Hi! I’m April Baik, an undergraduate student at Brigham Young University pursuing a B.S. in Statistics with a Data Science Emphasis and a minor in Computer Science.
I’m particularly interested in artificial intelligence and statistical modeling, especially how data-driven methods can be used to develop and evaluate reliable AI systems.
Currently, I work as a Research Assistant, developing AI-powered tools to support programming education, and as a Teaching Assistant for Statistical Modeling I. Through these experiences, I’ve been exploring both the technical side of building AI applications and the statistical methods needed to evaluate their performance.
Outside of academics, I enjoy playing guitar, baking, drawing, and watching anime.

title: Exploring Earthquakes Around the World Using the USGS API
text:
When I took an earth science class in high school, I learned about tectonic plates and how earthquakes tend to occur near their boundaries. I found it interesting that some regions experience earthquakes more frequently than others, and how the characteristics of earthquakes may differ depending on their geographic locations.
One thing I became curious about was whether earthquakes have different magnitudes and depths depending on where they occur.


Earthquakes often occur near tectonic plate boundaries, but not all boundaries are the same.
Japan and Peru are located near subduction zones, where one tectonic plate moves beneath another. These regions can experience earthquakes at various depths. On the other hand, California is located near a transform boundary, where two plates slide past each other horizontally. Earthquakes associated with this type of boundary are generally shallow.



One plane sinks under another in the subduction zone and two plates slide past each other sideways in the transform boundary.


Based on these differences, I wanted to explore whether earthquake characteristics differ across these regions.

2. Research Question
My main research question is:
How do earthquake magnitudes and depths differ across Japan, California, and Peru?

title: Exploring Earthquakes Around the World Using the USGS API
text:
3. Ethical Considerations
Before collecting the data, I reviewed the USGS API documentation to understand how the API works and what parameters are supported.
USGS-produced data are government data that are publicly available for reuse, and USGS requests acknowledgment as the original source. I will be using API filters to request only the records needed for my research question and to avoid putting unnecessary load on their servers.
I will provide a link to the original data source and share my Python code so others can reproduce the collection process.

title: Exploring Earthquakes Around the World Using the USGS API
section: 4. Collecting Earthquake Data Using an API
text:
4. Collecting Earthquake Data Using an API
For this project, I used the USGS Earthquake Catalog API, provided by the United States Geological Survey (USGS).
The API provides information about global earthquakes, including magnitude, depth, geographic location, and occurrence time. Using the API, I can filter earthquake records by date, magnitude, and geographic coordinates and scrape only the variables I need. It also makes the process structured and reproducible.
I chose this API because it provides individual observations of the earthquake and this helps us interpret the trend of the earthquakes.

Making an API Request
I used Python’s requests library to send GET requests to the API. The API returns earthquake records in GeoJSON format, which contains information about each earthquake.
For this project, I collected earthquakes that occurred between January 1 – June 1, 2025 in Japan, Peru, and California, which has minimum magnitude of 4.0. I selected the regions by defining specific latitude and longitude for the areas that are scraped.

import requests
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pathlib import Path
url = "https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/query"

regions = {
    "Japan": (24, 46, 123, 146),
    "California": (32, 42, -125, -114),
    "Peru": (-19, 1, -82, -68)
}

# Store raw earthquake records
raw_earthquakes = []

for region in regions:
    min_lat, max_lat, min_lon, max_lon = regions[region]
    params = {
        "format": "geojson",
        "starttime": "2025-01-01",
        "endtime": "2025-06-01",
        "minmagnitude": 4.0,
        "minlatitude": min_lat,
        "maxlatitude": max_lat,
        "minlongitude": min_lon,
        "maxlongitude": max_lon
    }
    response = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=30)
    response.raise_for_status()

    data = response.json()

    for event in data["features"]:
        raw_earthquakes.append({
            "region": region,
            "event": event
        })
    print(region, len(data["features"]))

Japan 373
California 11
Peru 142


I also used error checking and request timeouts to avoid leaving unsuccessful requests running indefinitely.
The API parameters allowed me to filter earthquake records by date, magnitude, and geographic location.


Preparing the Dataset
After collecting the raw data, I converted the earthquake records into a DataFrame.
The GeoJSON response contains a list called features, where each feature represents an earthquake. I extracted information from the properties and geometry sections of each event.

earthquakes = []

for record in raw_earthquakes:
    event = record["event"]
    properties = event["properties"]
    coordinates = event["geometry"]["coordinates"]

    earthquakes.append({
        "id": event["id"],
        "region": record["region"],
        "location": properties["place"],
        "magnitude": properties["mag"],
        "depth": coordinates[2],
        "latitude": coordinates[1],
        "longitude": coordinates[0],
        "date": pd.to_datetime(
            properties["time"],
            unit="ms",
            utc=True
        )
    })

earthquake_data = pd.DataFrame(earthquakes)
earthquake_data = earthquake_data.loc[:,["id","region", "magnitude", "depth", "latitude", "longitude","date"]]
earthquake_data["date"] = earthquake_data["date"].dt.date

print(earthquake_data.isna().sum())
print(earthquake_data.duplicated().sum())

print(earthquake_data.head())

Looking at the scatterplot, the earthquakes from California are focused on the left bottom of the plot, having depth around 0-10 km and magnitude mainly around 4.0-5.0. The earthquakes from Peru has a wider range of depth and magnitude, having magnitude between 4.0-6.0 and depth mainly between 0-300km. The earthquakes from Japan have the most spread observations, having magnitude between 4.0-7.0 and depth between 0-600 km.
Although there are a few outliers for each regions, California have the least earthquakes with comparatively less magnitude and depth. Peru and Japan have earthquakes that have magnitude larger than 5.0 and the depth are extremely deeper compared to earthquakes in California.
Although these plots cannot fully explain the geological causes of earthquakes, they help us understand that Japan and Peru have a higher occurrence and severity of earthquakes.

title: Choosing Features and Targets in Machine Learning
text:
When training a model in machine learning, we need to answer two important questions:

What information should the model use to make predictions?
What are we trying to predict?

These questions introduce two fundamental concepts in supervised machine learning: features and targets.
In this tutorial, we will learn how to identify features and targets, separate them using Python’s pandas library, and avoid common mistakes when choosing variables for a prediction problem.
In machine learning, a model learns patterns from data containing input variables and known outcomes.

Features: input variables which a model uses to make predictions. They provide information that could help explain and predict an outcome. It id also called predictors.
Target: variable which we want the model to predict. It is also called the response variable or dependent variable.

We can describe this relationship using linear model:
\(Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{i1}+\beta_2X_{i2}+\beta_3X_{i3}+\varepsilon_i\)
In machine learning, features are represented by X, and the target is represented by Y. 
An important distinction is that a variable is not automatically a feature or target based on its name or data type. Its role depends on the prediction question.
Features give the algorithm the patterns it uses to map input data to the target outcome, and the target shows what problem we are solving and whether the task is classification or regression. Reasonable features lead to high accuracy, and it is important to avoid overfitting.

3. Separating Features and Targets with pandas
Once we’ve identified our features and target, let’s separate them into different variables using pandas.
In machine learning, we commonly use X to represent the features and Y to represent the target.

X = data_for_model.loc[:,["YearRemodAdd", "Neighborhood", "GrLivArea"]]
Y = data_for_model.loc[:,"SalePrice"]

This tells us that X contains 1,460 observations and three features, while Y contains 1,460 target values.

Why Do We Separate X and Y?
Many machine-learning tools expect the features and target to be provided separately.
For example, a typical model in scikit-learn is trained using the following structure:
model.fit(X, Y)
Here, X contains the information used to learn patterns, while Y provides the known outcomes.
Furthermore, to train the model, our categorical feature Neighborhood would need to be encoded for many machine-learning algorithms.
The main takeaway is that separating X and Y is an essential preparation step before training a supervised machine-learning model.

title: Choosing Features and Targets in Machine Learning
text:
4. Choosing the Right Features
Identifying the target is usually straightforward once we know our prediction question. However, choosing appropriate features requires more consideration.
Let’s look at three important questions to ask when selecting features.

Does the Variable Contain Potentially Useful Information?
For our housing dataset, GrLivArea could be a useful feature because houses at higher level may tend to have higher selling prices.
Similarly, Neighborhood could provide useful information because house prices often vary depending on location. For example, houses in safe area with low-crime rate could be more expensive than houses in an area with high-crime rate.
When choosing features, we should consider whether each variable could help explain or predict the target.


Will This Information Be Available When Making Predictions?
Suppose we want to predict a house’s selling price before it is sold.
We can use information such as its living area, neighborhood, and remodeling year because these characteristics can be known before the sale.
However, we cannot use the final selling price itself as a feature because that information would not yet be available.
Using information that would not be available at prediction time can cause data leakage.
Data leakage occurs when information that should not be available to a model is used during training or evaluation. This can make the model appear more accurate than it would be when making predictions on new data.

title: Choosing Features and Targets in Machine Learning
text:
Conclusion
Understanding the difference between features and targets is an essential first step in building a supervised machine-learning model.
Remember:

Features (X) are the input variables used to make predictions.
The target (Y) is the outcome we want the model to predict.
A variable’s role depends on the prediction question.
Features can be numerical or categorical.
Not every available variable should automatically be included as a feature.

Your next step: Find another dataset on Kaggle, define your own prediction question, and use pandas to separate the features and target into X and Y.
Before building a model, ask yourself the two questions:
What am I trying to predict, and what information do I need to make a successful prediction?
Answering these questions will help you choose appropriate features and targets before moving on to model training.
